content: The selection process for studies was consistent but unclear in some cases, and this did not appear to introduce bias; therefore, no downgrading was applied. For the Ortho ELISA test, two out of five studies used convenience sampling, and one study included only healthy blood donors, leading to a two-point downgrade. For the Monolisa test, four out of five studies had unclear participant selection, and one study did not clarify whether the index and reference tests were conducted within 30 days. However, as there were no high-risk concerns for bias, no downgrading was applied. Regarding specificity, only one study provided data with unclear participant selection, resulting in a one-point downgrade due to the lack of data from studies with random or consecutive selection to assess potential selection bias. For the Lumispot test, both studies had unclear participant selection, and since no data from studies with random or consecutive selection were available for comparison, a one-point downgrade was applied. The Lumipulse test included only one study with unclear participant selection, leading to a one-point downgrade. The Hunan Jynda test had one study with unclear participant selection, one study that included only healthy blood donors (considered high-risk for bias), and one study where it was unclear if the index and reference tests were performed within 30 days. These factors collectively led to a one-point downgrade. For the Murex test, three out of four studies had unclear participant selection, but no other high-risk concerns for bias were identified, so no downgrading was applied. Unexplained heterogeneity in the remaining studies may be related to covariates such as HIV and HBV co-infections or HCV genotype, which could not be adjusted for due to limited data. Additionally, not all studies identified HCV antibody status or stratified by acute and chronic infection, which may contribute to higher false-negative rates for HCV core antigen (HCV cAg). The ARCHITECT studies showed little heterogeneity, so no downgrading was applied. For the Ortho ELISA, moderate heterogeneity was noted, primarily due to one outlier study, resulting in a one-point downgrade. For the Monolisa sensitivity outcome, heterogeneity between studies precluded meta-analysis, leading to a two-point downgrade. For specificity, only one study was available, preventing heterogeneity assessment, and a one-point downgrade was applied. For the Murex sensitivity outcome, excessive heterogeneity prevented data pooling, leading to a two-point downgrade. For specificity, insufficient studies were available for meta-analysis, and heterogeneity could not be formally assessed, but a broad range of results led to a one-point downgrade. The EIKEN Lumispot test was used in only two studies, which showed similar sensitivity, indicating little heterogeneity, so no downgrading was applied. For the Fujirebio Lumipulse test, only one study was available, preventing heterogeneity assessment, and a one-point downgrade was applied. All studies were conducted in reference laboratories, primarily in highand middle-income countries, which may not represent the limited-resource settings for which these guidelines are intended. As a result, all tests were downgraded by one point. Imprecision was considered present when pooled confidence intervals exceeded 10% or when fewer than 250 samples were included in the analysis. Consequently, the Ortho ELISA and Hunan Jynda tests were downgraded one point for wide confidence intervals, and the Lumispot test was downgraded one point for small sample size. Imprecision could not be graded for the Monolisa specificity outcome or the Lumipulse test due to the inclusion of only one study. Dried blood spot (DBS) testing offers several advantages, including stability under high temperatures and humidity, reduced biohazard risk, easier transport, and the elimination of the need for venipuncture. This method increases access to testing, particularly in remote settings or among key populations such as people who inject drugs or prisoners. However, prolonged storage at high temperatures and humidity may negatively affect accuracy. DBS testing may require higher cut-offs to maintain sensitivity due to the small blood volume used, potentially reducing the ability to rule out HBV or HCV in some cases. Additionally, DBS is not yet regulatory-approved for HBV surface antigen (HBsAg), HCV antibody (HCV Ab), HBV DNA, or HCV RNA testing, and there is no manufacturer guidance on its use with commercial assays. Operational research is needed to evaluate the accuracy of DBS under real-world conditions, validate its use with commercially available tests, and determine appropriate cut-off values. Further studies are required to assess the degradation of HCV RNA in DBS samples stored at ambient temperatures and high humidity, particularly in HIV co-infected patients and for treatment monitoring. Systematic reviews on the limits of detection (LOD) for HCV RNA and HBV DNA testing on DBS are also necessary to capture all individuals requiring treatment or failing therapy. HCV core antigen (HCV cAg) testing has been developed as an alternative to nucleic acid testing (NAT) for diagnosing active HCV infection. While HCV cAg testing is less costly and complex than NAT, it requires sophisticated laboratory equipment and skilled staff. It may also misclassify individuals on antiviral treatment as responding when they have persistent low-level viremia below the assay's detection limits. Despite these limitations, HCV cAg testing could increase access to treatment and reduce disease progression and mortality in resource-limited settings.
